description: OsirisZk is a student-led space technology team from Altıeylül BİLSEM, Türkiye, supported by a mathematics educator. Our strengths include FPV drone systems, flight simulation, coding, and mathematical modeling. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to develop an interactive Mars exploration mission game that combines realistic flight physics, scientific data, and mission planning. We welcome collaborators interested in aerospace, robotics, software, and planetary exploration.
summary: We're Team OsirisZK, a group of students from Altıeylül BİLSEM in Balıkesir, Türkiye. Ingenuity really inspired us: it was planned for 5 flights and ended up flying 72. But it lived alone in the open, with no shelter and no way to be repaired, and in the end that's what stopped it. So we asked ourselves: what if the helicopter lived on the rover? We designed a 45 kg rover that carries a 1.8 kg helicopter on a docking pad. The pad locks the helicopter in place, charges it, swaps its battery and sends its data to Earth. Then we built a 3D browser game set in Jezero Crater to test the design. The weather in the game comes from real Perseverance MEDA data, so wind, dust devils and dust storms decide whether you can fly. The rover drives at Perseverance's real speed, the rotors follow real physics, and small AI models help the autopilot decide when to come home. Anyone can play it for free, without installing anything.
details:
What it does

Our project has two parts: a design for a rover-and-helicopter team, and a game where you can test that design on Mars. In the game you fly the helicopter off the rover's back, scan three rocks (hematite, sedimentary and basalt), bring the data back, land on the pad and send everything to Earth. You can fly it yourself with a keyboard, a gamepad or a touchscreen, or press one button and watch the autopilot do the whole mission.

How it works

We tried to make every number come from something real:

- Rotor power uses momentum theory, and we calibrated it to Ingenuity.

- Air density comes from MEDA pressure and temperature, about 0.017 kg/m³ in Jezero. If the rotors would need more than 2700 rpm, the game doesn't let you take off.

- The battery loses capacity in the cold: 44.4 Wh at 25 °C, but only 38.8 Wh at 0 °C.

- The rover uses terramechanics models (Bekker, Mohr–Coulomb, Janosi–Hanamoto), so it slips on sand and can get stuck in dust.

- The rover moves at Perseverance's real top speed, 4.2 cm/s. That is really slow, so we added a time-lapse option (×10 to ×100) to keep the game fun.

- Rocks are solid. Small rocks lift the wheels, big rocks stop the rover, and the helicopter can't fly through them.

The weather uses MEDA data from sols 105–110. It includes gusts, wind that gets stronger with height, moving dust devils and dust storms. In a storm the solar panels make less power, visibility drops and dust builds up on the panels.

We also added AI:

- an energy model that learns while the helicopter flies and tells the autopilot when it's time to go back;

- a GRU neural network that forecasts temperature;

- a small quantum machine learning classifier (4 qubits, simulated in the browser).

We were honest about the results. The GRU beat a simple daily-cycle baseline for temperature (0.37 °C vs 0.41 °C error), but not for pressure. The quantum model reached 96.3% accuracy with only 28 parameters, but the normal neural network still won with 99.3%.

Benefits and impact

On Mars, a helicopter that can recharge, get a fresh battery and hide from storms could keep scouting routes and finding science targets for years instead of months. On Earth, the same rover-plus-drone idea could help in disaster areas or high-altitude rescue. And for students like us, the game is a fun way to learn what Wh, W and rpm really mean, using real NASA data.

Tools we used

We wrote the game in plain JavaScript and WebGL2, with no game engine and no external libraries, so it runs offline in Chrome or Edge. We used Python for the data and machine learning scripts and Netlify for hosting. The game works in English and Turkish, and we check it with an automated browser test suite of more than 160 checks.

What makes it creative

Most Mars games are either realistic or fun. We wanted both: real Mars weather and real physics, but also a mission you can finish in a few minutes. The idea of the rover as a "garage" for the helicopter came from asking one simple question: why did Ingenuity's mission end?

What we considered

Weight was the biggest factor, because landing one kilogram on Mars costs roughly $0.24–2.4 million. We set design rules: thrust/weight of at least 1.5, rotor tip speed below Mach 0.8, and no single flight using more than 60% of the battery. We also thought about cold, dust, communication with Earth and cost. Our rough estimate for landing the 46.8 kg system is $204–304 million. Any values we couldn't measure are marked as ASSUMPTION in the code.
